title: The Singhpuria misl

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nishanwalia misl, the band that carried the Dal Khalsa's standard. Your line was the flag-bearers. What did you carry for someone? Today, the band of a man who carried a fan. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

The man with the fan. Earlier on this path you met him at Amritsar, moving the air over the sangat on a hot day, when the title of nawab found him. Nawab Kapur Singh went on to lead the Khalsa through the hard years. But the title came to a man who already had home ground. He had his own village, and his own riders, and they had a name. Today, not the title and not the fan. Today: the Singhpuria misl.
screen: `THE MAN WITH THE FAN.` → `A LEADER OF EVERYONE.` → `AND HIS OWN RIDERS.`

segments.voice: Three pieces. The first is a renamed village. Tradition says Kapur Singh took a village called Faizullapur, near Amritsar, and renamed it Singhpura, the town of the Singhs. His band took the new name: the Singhpurias. Some histories still call them by the old name too, the Faizullapurias. So the misl's name holds a small act of claiming: a village renamed for the Khalsa. The second piece is the size of the band. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Singhpuria misl was not among the great misls in riders or land. And that's the surprise. The man who held the title of nawab, the man the chiefs followed through the hard century, led a modest band of his own. He could have used his place at the head of the Khalsa to make his own riders the strongest. Tradition doesn't remember him doing that. The third piece is who came after him. When Kapur Singh grew old, tradition says, the leadership of the whole Khalsa did not pass to his own band. It went to Jassa Singh, from the Ahluwalias, the rider he had trained. His own misl carried on under its own chiefs, and the leadership of everyone went where he judged it should go. That's an unusual kind of leader. A nawab whose band stayed modest. A chief who handed the biggest job outside his own circle. Sikh histories dwell on his humility: the fan, the stables, the robe touched to the feet of five Sikhs. The Singhpuria misl is the same humility, written in the map. It's the nawab's band.
screen: `FAIZULLAPUR RENAMED SINGHPURA.` · `A MODEST BAND FOR A NAWAB.` · `THE LEADERSHIP PASSED OUTSIDE IT.` · `HUMILITY WRITTEN IN THE MAP.` · then, large: `THE NAWAB'S BAND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something you passed on. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you could have kept something for yourself and handed it to someone else instead: a seat, a role, the last slice, a job you let a newer person try. Or a time you held on. Don't judge either. Let the moment come back: what it cost you, and what it gave them. On each breath, let it sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

The Singhpuria misl. Nawab Kapur Singh's own band, named for the village he renamed Singhpura. This week: the Ramgarhias, the Kanhaiyas, the Sukerchakias, the Nakais, the Dallewalias, the Nishanwalias, and the Singhpurias. Today's word.
Your line: the nawab's band. Today, when you could take credit for something, hand it to someone else on your team. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Nawab Kapur Singh in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader known for seva, and the Singhpuria misl as the band that came from his village.

notes: This day avoids retelling day 852 (the fan and the title) and recalls it in a line.
Faizullapur renamed Singhpura by Kapur Singh, and 'Singhpura' glossed as 'the town of the Singhs': confirm.
'Not among the great misls' is a comparative claim framed as Sikh histories' telling; confirm or cut.
Leadership of the Dal Khalsa passing to Jassa Singh Ahluwalia rather than within the Singhpuria misl (which passed to his nephew Khushal Singh in common accounts, not named here): confirm.
'The robe touched to the feet of the Five' recalls day 852's telling ('five respected Sikhs'); confirm wording.
Week-end recap in the word segment lists the index titles for days 890–896.
Editor: 'the feet of the Five' changed to 'five Sikhs' to match day 852 and avoid implying the Panj Piare.

Audit: Kapur Singh is usually said to have been born at Kaloke and to have taken Faizullapur (near Amritsar) and renamed it Singhpura; the voice no longer says he came from Faizullapur. Practice rewritten (it duplicated day 889's thank-a-good-leader practice); hook line changed to stop echoing day 889's 'lead everyone'; 'Sikhs remember his humility first' softened to Sikh histories.
